stem: You have recently completed an evaluation of a 5-year-old boy in foster care who is diagnosed with a neuromuscular disorder which will worsen over time. Your opinion is that he does not have difficulty learning and is ready for school. During treatment planning, you are asked by child welfare services to participate in educational planning at the boy’s school. Of the following, when making recommendations at the meeting, the BEST approach would be to:

options.html: Discuss his case only with the teacher and principal present
Have the boy talk about his physical limitations
Make educational recommendations and ask the school to monitor fatigue and motor skills
Obtain caregiver permission, and discuss the boy’s history and diagnosis and their effect on his performance

answer:
The correct answer is E.

From 04 - School Age. For a child with a chronic condition, the lecture's school-readiness role includes explaining the effect of illness on school performance to educators, so the school can plan for a disorder that will progress. His information is confidential, and for a child in foster care the consent to share it comes from the legal caregiver (child welfare or the foster parents). The best approach is therefore to get that permission first, then give the history, diagnosis and their expected effect on performance.

  • A narrows the audience but still shares without consent.
  • B puts a 5-year-old in charge of explaining his own disease.
  • C he has no learning difficulty, so insisting on comprehensive services overshoots.
  • D gives recommendations without the context the school needs to apply them.

stem: In which of the following situations would a diagnosis of ADHD be most appropriate?

options.html: A 9-year-old boy presenting with inattentive symptoms that affect academic performance but is otherwise thriving socially and his parents report no concerns in the home environment

A 7-year-old girl who presents due to parental concerns about inattentive and hyperactive symptoms in the home, but previous report cards and a completed SNAP-IV scale by the current teacher give no indication of ADHD symptomatology

A 10-year-old boy whose parents describe academic difficulties along with hyperactivity and impulsivity in the home that interfere with day-to-day function, with a review of report cards revealing evidence of hyperactivity, impulsivity, and inattention at school

An 8-year-old girl who has been hyperactive in multiple settings over the past three months, including a substantial deterioration in academic performance, but on history you learn that there has been domestic violence in the household over that time period

answer:
The correct answer is C.

Presence of inattentive and/or hyperactive symptoms that affect function in 2 or more settings (answer A and B only indicate symptoms/impairment in one environment); not better explained by another diagnosis (trauma/stressor-related disorder is better explanation than ADHD in answer D).

stem: Which of the following is consistent with what is known regarding the natural course of ADHD over the lifespan?

options.html: ADHD is associated with multiple symptoms and adverse outcomes in childhood and adolescence, but even though symptoms may persist into adulthood, there is little evidence of negative outcomes in adulthood
Untreated ADHD adversely affects academic performance in children but it does not have an impact on peer relationships or social function
Untreated ADHD is associated with increased risk of legal issues and high school dropout in adolescence
Suicidal ideation is common in children with untreated ADHD

answer:
The correct answer is C.

Impairment occurs across the lifespan (so A is false); childhood ADHD can contribute to social difficulties and poor self-esteem (so B is false); although behavioural disturbance is possible in children with ADHD, suicidal ideation is rare (so D is false).

lectureMeta: The week's Readiness Assessment, as it was sat.
stem: Which of the following statements is correct about action potentials?

options.html: Action potentials are transient changes of the resting membrane potential characterized by the opening of voltage-gated ion channels.
Three phases characterize action potentials: depolarization, repolarization and inactivation phases.
The opening of the voltage-gated potassium channels brings the membrane to positive potential values.
Changes in the concentration of ions in the plasma don’t affect action potentials' generation.
The refractory periods restore ions' concentration gradients, allowing for action potentials to be triggered on demand.

answer:
The correct answer is A.

In the nerve cells, action potentials are characterized by the transient opening of voltagegated sodium channels, leading to a rapid depolarization of the cell membrane. In other excitable cells, other ion channels contribute to the generation of action potentials. The 3 key phases of an action potential are depolarization, repolarization and hyperpolarization. In each of these phases, we observe the opening, closing and inactivation (when applicable) of specific channels. The electrochemical gradient for potassium drives this ion out of the cells when its channels are opened. When positive charges leave the cells, the membrane potential becomes more negative. Changes in the concentration of ions in the plasma do affect the generation of action potentials. For example, increasing the plasma concentration of potassium favours the depolarization of excitable cells. The refractory periods are essential to control the frequency of action potentials per unit of time. The sodium-potassium pump restores the gradient of these ions, allowing action potentials to proceed uninterruptedly (at a frequency limited by the refractory periods).

lectureMeta: The week's Readiness Assessment, as it was sat.
stem: Which of the graphs represents a situation of hyperkalemia? A. B.
answer:
The correct answer is A.

If the concentration of potassium is increased there will be less potassium leaving the neurons through the leak channels. With more potassium in the outside, the concentration gradient is reduced, and K will be less willing to leave the cell. The net result is accumulation of positive charges inside the cell which brings the membrane potential closer to the threshold. Therefore, this neuron is more likely to fire an AP. If, for some reason, the levels of K are low, the membrane potential will be shifted to more negative values. With lower levels of K in the ECF, the chemical gradient for this ion has increased, favoring K to leave the cell. With more K leaving, the membrane becomes hyperpolarized and in order to have the same action, the stimulus needs to be stronger.

lectureMeta: The week's Readiness Assessment, as it was sat.
stem: In demyelinating diseases such as Multiple Sclerosis the propagation of the action potential, in certain areas of the nervous system, will progressively become slower. Which of the following statements better explains the slower conduction of the action potential in this condition?

options.html: The loss of myelin affects the release of neurotransmitters by the neurons
The loss of myelin results in increased membrane resistance
The loss of myelin prevents the leakage of ions to the ECF
The loss of myelin results in loss of saltatory conduction

answer:
The correct answer is D.

the presence of myelin does not affect the release of neurotransmitter. Myelin increases the membrane resistance by preventing potassium ions from moving out of the cell; a process that speeds up the conductance of an action potential. The presence of myelin forces the positive charges to move rapidly throughout the axon. These charges depolarize the next axonal segment that is covered by myelin strengthening the action potential being conducted. The new incoming positive charges will then “jump” to the next node. This saltatory conduction speeds up the propagation of an action potential. Thus, the loss of myelin in degenerative diseases such as MS, leads to slower and impaired conduction.

lectureMeta: The week's Readiness Assessment, as it was sat.
stem: If the voltage-gated sodium channels in the motor end plate were blocked, which of the following events would be impaired?

options.html: the release of acetylcholine by the motor neuron
the generation of the end plate potentials by the motor end plate
the opening of the voltage-gated calcium channels in the axon terminal
the activation of the nicotinic receptors in the motor end plate
the generation of an action potential by the muscle fiber

answer:
The correct answer is E.

If we were able to specifically inhibit the VG-sodium channels in the motor end plate, no action potential would be generated by the muscle fiber. This inhibition would not affect the release of acetylcholine or the opening of the VG-calcium channels as these processes are happening in the pre-synaptic cell. If the release of ACh is normal, then the nicotinic receptors in motor end plate will be activated and the muscle will be able to generate an end plate potential. However, since the VG-sodium channels are blocked, the EPPs won’t lead to an action potential.

lectureMeta: The week's Readiness Assessment, as it was sat.
stem: Marina, a 27-year-old woman, was admitted to the hospital presenting nausea, vomiting, generalized muscle weakness that progressed to paralysis and difficulty swallowing. Laboratory tests showed infection by Clostridium botulinum. Which of the following statements best describes the physiological basis of the muscle weakness & paralysis caused by the botulinum toxin?

options.html: Blockage of acetylcholine release by the motor neurons
Competitive inhibition of the acetylcholinesterase enzyme
Enhanced activity of the calcium pump in the muscle fiber
Enhanced activity of the transporter that recycles choline back into the axon terminal

answer:
The correct answer is B.

Acetylcholine is the primary neurotransmitter of the neuromuscular junction. This is the neurotransmitter that, upon binding to its nicotinic receptor, initiates the endplate potential that will trigger action potentials resulting in muscle contraction. If a toxin prevents the release of this neurotransmitter, muscle weakness will occur. Inhibiting acetylcholinesterase activity can also lead to muscle weakness and paralysis if the body cannot overcome this inhibition. That is what we see with pesticides that bind irreversibly to this enzyme. Excessive amounts of acetylcholine can lead to desensitization and inactivation of the nicotinic receptors. This option is somewhat correct, but option B best explains the muscle weakness & paralysis in this case. The calcium ATPase or calcium pump located in the sarcoplasmic reticulum act by pumping calcium back into the reticulum. This is a mechanism by which the muscle cells “relax”. Enhancing the activity of this pump would potentially decrease the force of contraction, but it would not prevent muscle contraction. The reuptake of choline and acetate (acetylcholine products) is limited by the capacity of the transporter but also the number of molecules available. If diet and the release if acetylcholine remains the same, enhancing the activity of the choline transporter should not cause muscle weakness & paralysis. If only specific motor units were blocked, we would most likely observe localized and not generalized weakness & paralysis.

stem: You are in a clinic seeing a previously healthy 30-year old who is presenting with abdominal pain and distension. She had a high blood pressure reading (140/ 90). Her other vitals are stable. She is very worried as she recalls that her mother had similar presentation before she was diagnosed with Autosomal Dominant polycystic kidney disease. What is her chance of having that genetic condition (based on the mode of inheritance)?
answer:
The correct answer is C.

Answer is 50% as it is an autosomal dominant condition

From 02 - Genetics. The mother had ADPKD, an autosomal dominant condition, and the note gives the rule: a 1 in 2 (50%) chance that each child inherits the trait, males and females equally. Her hypertension and abdominal distension raise suspicion, but the question asks only for the inheritance-based prior risk.

  • A (1%) is the gonadal-mosaicism recurrence risk after a de novo mutation, but here the mother is affected.
  • B (25%) applies to autosomal recessive inheritance from two carrier parents.
  • D (75%) would need both parents affected.

stem: What is the karyotype for Klinefelter Syndrome?
answer:
The correct answer is B.

From 07 - Chromosome Disorder Testing. Klinefelter syndrome is 47,XXY: an extra X in a male, giving tall stature, gynecomastia, small testes, learning disability and infertility with a normal appearance. The other options are the other syndromes in the lecture's table:

  • A 45,X = Turner syndrome (webbed neck, coarctation, short stature, primary amenorrhea).
  • C trisomy 13 = Patau (midline defects, cleft palate, polydactyly).
  • D trisomy 18 = Edward (rocker-bottom feet, overlapping fingers, cardiac defects).

B is the intended answer only if it reads 47,XXY.

stem: Which of those conditions is an example of Autosomal Recessive disorder?
answer:
The correct answer is A.

From 02 - Genetics. Autosomal recessive disorders need two variant alleles: affected children usually appear in one sibship of one generation with unaffected carrier parents, males and females equally, and consanguinity raises the chance. The lecture gives cystic fibrosis (CFTR, ΔF508) as the classic example, so A.

  • B Patau syndrome is trisomy 13, a numerical chromosome abnormality (aneuploidy), not a single-gene disorder.
  • C Turner syndrome is 45,X, a monosomy.
  • D Down syndrome is trisomy 21, usually from nondisjunction in meiosis I.

The discriminator: Mendelian inheritance patterns describe single genes; the three distractors are whole-chromosome errors.

stem: You are seeing a 33-year old who is coming in for her routine check-up. She has a son with Duchenne muscular dystrophy. She was found to be carrier for the DMD mutation that was identified for her son. How is Duchenne muscular dystrophy inherited?
answer:
The correct answer is A.

From 02 - Genetics. The note names Duchenne muscular dystrophy as its example of X-linked inheritance: males are affected almost exclusively because they are hemizygous, and the variant passes from female carriers to sons. That is exactly this family, a carrier mother with an affected son.

  • B (AD) would make the carrier mother affected herself.
  • C (mitochondrial) would give disease to all her children regardless of sex, and involves mtDNA, not a nuclear gene like DMD.
  • D (AR) would need the father to be a carrier too, and would not favour sons.

stem: What is her chance of having another child with that diagnosis?

options.html: All of her daughters will be affected
All of her daughters will be carriers
All of her sons will be affected
She has a 50% chance of passing that mutation to her children

answer:
The correct answer is D.

From 02 - Genetics. A carrier mother has one normal and one DMD-variant X, and each child receives one of them at random. So each child has a 50% chance of inheriting the variant. The note's breakdown by sex: 50% of sons affected and 50% of daughters carriers.

  • B overstates it: half of daughters are carriers, not all. “All daughters carriers” is the rule for an affected father.

That people with disabilities should not have children
That she should not worry about these things until she gets older
The role of folic acid in neural tube defects

The correct answer is A.

Beginning a longer-acting stimulant that is taken once daily
Developing a treatment plan with his parents without his input
Refusing to see the patient because he stopped the medication without consulting you

The correct answer is B.

Adolescents become responsible for their own medical care as they learn independence skills - simplifying medication regimens to fit with the adolescent's personal schedule and goals will improve adherence. ADHD persists into adulthood.

stem: In 2007, investigators wish to study the effects of exposure to polyvinyl chloride on solid tumor cancer risk. They use personnel files obtained from chemical companies for the period 1950 - 1990 to assign employees a PVC exposure score, based on where they worked in the plants and for how long. They use telephone interviews, tumor registries, death certificates and physician billing data to measure cancers diagnosed between 1955 and 2007. This most closely resembles which research design?
answer:
The correct answer is C.

The investigators did not assign exposure, therefore it’s an Observational design. However they did start by determining who had been exposed, therefore it’s a Cohort design. And they went back into past records to gather the necessary study data, therefore it’s a Retrospective Cohort design.

answer:
The correct answer is D.

Randomization is the only study design technique that attempts to balance confounders (both known an unknown) equally between the two comparison groups in a trial.

The entire outer ear (auricle) from the head
The lobule of the outer ear (auricle) from the rest of the auricle
The tip of the nose from the rest of the nose and face

stem: Which of the following would be a contraindication for a patient to have an MRI?
answer:
The correct answer is C.

The powerful magnetic field may cause damage to implanted devices such as cardiac pacemakers and cochlear implants and thus patients with these devices are contraindicated from MR imaging.

lectureMeta: The week's Self-Assessment, as it was released.
stem: Which of the following organ systems is responsible for returning excess interstitial fluid to systemic circulation?
answer:
The correct answer is D.

Tissue fluid arises from blood filtered through the capillary walls and consists of the small molecules of blood plasma, including water, various ions, nutrient molecules, and respiratory gases. For complex reasons slightly more fluid exits from the arteriole end of each capillary bed than reenters the blood at the venule end. The lymphatic vessels function to collect this excess tissue fluid from the loose connective tissue around capillaries and return it to the bloodstream.

stem: A young boy uses his right hand to screw-in a light bulb. Which of the following terms best describes the screw-home movement of his forearm?
answer:
The correct answer is E.

The screw-home mechanism is the clockwise motion that drives a screw into a receptacle. When using the right hand, the palm and forearm turn laterally and the palm moves from facing posterior to facing anterior, which is supination.

Form the outer barrier of the surface of the body
Support other tissues by conveying blood vessels and nerves
Carry the nerve cell processes to a target muscle
Form the contractile unit of skeletal muscles such as biceps brachii

stem: What are the three basic components from which all types of connective tissue are constructed?

options.html: Fibroblasts, adipocytes, and mesenchymal stem cells

answer:
The correct answer is D.

D is correct as all types of connective tissue have varying proportions of cell, fibers and non-fiber components to meet the demand of the specific type of connective tissue. For example, dense regular connective tissue is packed with fibers with few cells and little nonfiber components.

stem: A man decides to use a utility knife to cut through a plastic pipe. His hand slips and he cuts the tip of his pinky finger completely off. A surgeon may be able to reattach the fingertip and restore skeletal muscle function in the fingertip providing the following healing occurs:

options.html: Neurons divide and Schwann cells proliferate
Oligodendrocytes proliferate and nerve fibers grow
Nerve fibers grow and Schwann cells proliferate
Nerve fibers grow and Schwann cells secrete neurotransmitters
Schwann cells and astrocytes migrate into the damage are

answer:
The correct answer is C.

C is correct as the axon of peripheral nerves that are severed have the capacity to grow and extend nerve fibers into a conduit formed from proliferating Schwann cells. If all goes well the nerve fiber will innervate the distal muscle restoring function.

lectureMeta: The week's Self-Assessment, as it was released.
stem: Which of the following concerning the hyperpolarizing phase of the action potential is correct?

options.html: It occurs due to increased activity of the Na+/K+ pump
It is a result of sodium inactivation gate closing
It is caused by the diffusion of calcium (Ca++) out of the cell
The membrane potential approaches the K+ equilibrium potential
It is caused by the diffusion of Na+ out of the cell

answer:
The correct answer is D.

the exit of potassium out of the neuronal cell, down its concentration gradient, is the main event responsible for the hyperpolarization of the cell membrane.

stem: The following is the best description of osteoclasts

options.html: Cells that differentiate into osteoblasts that deposit bone matrix
Multinucleated cells that are derived from monocytes and resorb bone
Multinucleated cells that differentiate into osteocytes found in lacunae
Multinucleated cells that are derived from osteoblasts and resorb bone

answer:
The correct answer is C.

From 06 - Connective Tissue. The note describes the osteoclast as formed by the fusion of peripheral blood monocytes/macrophages, multinucleated (up to 30 nuclei), secreting acid and metalloproteinases that resorb bone in Howship's lacunae. Every element of C is there.

  • A describes the osteoblast, which becomes an osteocyte once enclosed in matrix.
  • B describes the osteoprogenitor cell, which differentiates into bone-depositing osteoblasts.
  • D mixes the osteoclast's nuclei with the osteocyte's location; osteocytes are single cells in lacunae derived from osteoblasts.
  • E has the right function but the wrong origin: osteoclasts come from the monocyte line, not from osteoblasts.

stem: Which of the following describes the correct role of the components of the control systems that regulate body temperature?

options.html: the effector detects the actual body temperature
the comparator/control centre receives signals directly from the effector
the controlled variable is the skeletal muscle and blood vessels
temperature sensors send signals directly to the effector
high levels of the controlled variable shut off the effector through the comparator/control centre

answer:
The correct answer is E.

In the negative feedback control of body temperature, the sensors detect the change in temperature, which is the controlled variable; the control centre receives signals from the sensors (not effectors) and once the temperature is back to normal, the effectors are shut off via the control centre.

The correct answer is C.

Typically, in dehydration, there is more loss of fluids than electrolytes; this results in decreased ECF volume which increases its osmolarity. After osmotic equilibrium, both ECF and ICF compartments will have decreased volume and increased osmolality (option C).

answer:
The correct answer is D.

The ingestion of isotonic saline will result in increased ECF volume but no change in osmolality. This is because isotonic saline has the same osmolarity as the ECF. Since the osmolarity of the ECF compartment is not changing, there won’t be significant changes in the volume and osmolarity for the ICF compartment. This is a way to replace ECF fluid loss. Diagram D.

stem: Cells may NOT be modified for specialized functions by:

increasing their surface area by forming microvilli for added absorption

undergoing cell fusion to establish large multinucleated cells

lectureMeta: The week's Self-Assessment, as it was released.
stem: Which of the following concerning skeletal muscle is correct?

options.html: Relaxation is due to passive Ca++ uptake by sarcoplasmic reticulum
Contraction is due to Ca++ release from T tubules
Contraction is due to Ca++ binding to tropomyosin
Z lines move apart during relaxation
The thin and thick myofilaments get shorter during a muscle contraction

answer:
The correct answer is D.

The uptake of calcium by the sarcoplasmic reticulum (SR) is mediated by an active transporter. This process required ATP and thus, it is not passive. The T-tubules propagate the depolarization of the membrane (action potential) that will open the calcium channels in the SR. Calcium is released from the SR not the T tubules. Ca++ binds to troponin causing tropomyosin to roll off myosin binding sites found on actin. Myosin attaches to Actin (crossbridge formation) and power stroke occurs. Actin (thin filaments) slides over Myosin (thick filaments) and muscle contracts (sliding filaments – sarcomeres shorten). The length of the myofilaments (thin and thick) doesn’t change but the sarcomeres shorten during muscle contraction.

answer:

From 01 - Biochemistry. The note says proteins are made of 20 or 21 amino acids, and lists amino acids among the essential micromolecules that combine to form macromolecules.

  • B (monosaccharides) build carbohydrates such as glycogen and starch.
  • C (nucleotides) build the nucleic acids DNA and RNA.
  • D (peptides) are short chains of amino acids, already assembled; they are a stage of protein structure, not the basic unit.
  • E (fatty acids) are the simplest lipids, stored as triglycerides.

stem: A baby has tested positive for one of the disorders on the provincial newborn screening test. Which of the following statements is correct?

options.html: The baby needs to be clinically assessed and undergo definitive testing to determine whether the baby is affected
Most diseases on the newborn screening panel are so rare that there is very little likelihood of the baby being affected
If only one mutation is found in the gene causing the disorder, then the baby is not affected
The baby is affected and needs to be started on therapy immediately to prevent complications
The provincial newborn screening test is designed to detect disorders which are particularly prevalent in Ontario

answer:
The correct answer is A.

Screening tests are not diagnostic. We need to assess.

From 05 - Genetic Screening. Newborn screening detects babies at risk; it is NOT diagnostic, and screens carry false positives. A positive result therefore means clinical assessment plus definitive testing before anyone is labelled affected.

  • B wrong: a positive screen raises the probability; it is never dismissed because the disease is rare.
  • C wrong: one variant in a recessive gene usually means a carrier, but 02 - Genetics notes that two variants on different alleles (trans) cause disease, a second variant can be missed, and not every panel disorder is recessive.
  • D wrong: it treats a screen as a diagnosis.
  • E wrong: disorders are chosen by the Wilson and Jungner criteria (serious, asymptomatic stage, treatable), not by Ontario prevalence.

stem: You see a 5-year-old girl with severe global developmental delay to determine if there could be an underlying genetic syndrome. You decide to order chromosomal microarray. Which of the following chromosome differences will NOT be detected by microarray?

options.html: A 500kb duplication in the DMD gene

answer:
The correct answer is C.

A microarray will not detect a balanced translocation

From 07 - Chromosome Disorder Testing. The lecture's organising idea: a karyotype shows chromosome structure, including balanced rearrangements, while a microarray shows gene content, that is, gains and losses. A balanced translocation such as t(11;22) moves material without adding or removing any (06 - Chromosomal Anomalies: “no missing information, but the information is shuffled”), so a microarray sees a normal dosage. It needs a karyotype.

  • A (Turner, 45,X) is a whole-chromosome loss, an obvious dosage change.
  • B (15q11.2 deletion) and E (500 kb DMD duplication) are submicroscopic copy-number changes, the imbalances microarray exists to find.
  • D (mosaic trisomy 21) is extra chromosome 21 material in a proportion of cells, still a gain in content.

From 08 - Developmental Milestones. Check each finding against the 18-month row and the red flags:

  • D normal: temper tantrums and high activity are expected from 18 to 36 months.

options.html: A combination of breast milk and infant formula

answer:

Breast is best for the first 6 months

From 10 - Infant Nutrition. The lecture recommends that babies are breastfed exclusively until 6 months of age, with breastfeeding continued up to 2 years. Term infants have adequate iron stores from the mother up to 6 months, which is why iron-rich solids are added only after that. Breastfed infants need vitamin D 400 IU/day (01 - Child Development).

  • C, D formula is an alternative when breastfeeding is not possible, not the recommendation; iron is also less well absorbed from formula.
  • E rice cereal is a solid food, introduced from about 6 months.

stem: Which of the following are potential consequences of dieting in adolescents:

options.html: Increased risk of developing an eating disorder

answer:
The correct answer is E.

All can be the sequelae of dieting.

From 06 - Adolescent Development. Every listed option is a recognised consequence of restrictive dieting, so “all of the above” (E):

  • A – energy restriction suppresses the reproductive axis, giving menstrual irregularity or amenorrhea.
  • B – undernutrition causes poor concentration, irritability and fatigue.
  • C – restriction drives a restrict-binge cycle.
  • D – dieting is a leading risk factor for developing an eating disorder.

The note's approach reflects this seriousness: ask how long the teen has been changing their eating to influence shape or weight, take lying and standing vitals, an ECG, and a broad panel of bloodwork.

From 09 - Introduction to Vaccines. The note's live attenuated viral vaccines are measles, oral polio, rotavirus, varicella and yellow fever, and live vaccines are contraindicated in the immunocompromised, pregnant women and neonates because they can cause vaccine-strain disease (C). Every other option is non-live:

lectureMeta: The student-written, instructor-approved bank built by the Class of 2024 Academic Directors (December 2020) and re-filed per week by the Meds 2025 volunteers.
stem: Which one of the following statements on diagnostic tools in incorrect?

options.html: Pathology involves the interpretation of cells and tissues.
Ultrasound does not expose the patient to radiation.
Microbiology identifies bacteria, viruses, and parasites.
X-ray, CT, and MRI produce signals based upon tissue density.
Biochemistry includes metabolic tests and tumour markers.

answer:
The correct answer is D.

MRI does not produce a signal based on tissue density, but instead on the prevalence of hydrogen atoms.

review.t: Tasks of a Physician - Applying Frameworks

lectureMeta: The student-written, instructor-approved bank built by the Class of 2024 Academic Directors (December 2020) and re-filed per week by the Meds 2025 volunteers.
stem: Which one of the following approaches is not in alignment with Choosing Wisely principles?

options.html: A patient presents with a concerning mole and is concerned about skin cancer. The physician performs a punch biopsy for pathologic diagnosis.
A patient presents with lower back pain since last week after moving heavy boxes. The physician orders an MRI for further investigation.

A patient with good overall health has no symptoms and wants blood tests to confirm that she does not have any unseen conditions. The physician emphasizes that there does not appear to be any concerns and does not run the blood tests.
A hospital implements a policy to reduce the number of pre-operative laboratory tests for low-risk surgeries to save both time and money, particularly when the tests do not change patient management.

answer:
The correct answer is B.

In the Choosing Wisely framework, the use of costly testing is avoided if it won’t change patient management. As well, other lower cost options should be followed in this scenario first before any expensive testing/investigation

stem: Which of the following is considered the strongest evidence in the context of evidence-based management plans?
answer:
The correct answer is D.

A systematic review analyzes many different peer-reviewed articles and is considered the strongest form of evidence in evidence-based decision making.

lectureMeta: The student-written, instructor-approved bank built by the Class of 2024 Academic Directors (December 2020) and re-filed per week by the Meds 2025 volunteers.
stem: Which of the following accurately describes the indicated strategy for prevention and disease control?

options.html: Primordial prevention is geared toward the entire population.
Primary prevention has the ultimate goal of reducing disease prevalence.
Tertiary prevention is geared toward people with one or more risk factors.
Secondary prevention intends to reduce complications for patients with advanced disease.
Health promotion applies mainly to patients with one or more risk factors.

answer:
The correct answer is A.

Primordial prevention (Health promotion) is geared toward the entire population with a goal of reducing risk factors.

lectureMeta: The student-written, instructor-approved bank built by the Class of 2024 Academic Directors (December 2020) and re-filed per week by the Meds 2025 volunteers.
stem: Two approaches for disease prevention include the clinical approach and the public health approach. Which of the following statements is incorrect?

options.html: The clinical approach identifies high-risk individuals and offers individual protection.
The public health approach may lead to poor motivation for individual patients.
The public health approach involves altering behaviours in the entire population.
The prevention paradox is the phenomenon that, with the public health approach, many people need to make changes that may only provide a relatively small benefit to individuals.
The clinical approach is effective in widespread reduction of disease incidence.

answer:
The correct answer is E.

The clinical approach involves treating individuals who have highly elevated risk factors or who already have a condition, but it is not as valuable in the widespread reduction of disease incidence.

lectureMeta: The student-written, instructor-approved bank built by the Class of 2024 Academic Directors (December 2020) and re-filed per week by the Meds 2025 volunteers.
stem: Concerning the epidemiological transition, which of the following statements is correct?

options.html: The typical life expectancy in the receding pandemics stage is >70 years.
The pestilence and famine stage is largely associated with malnutrition and infectious diseases.
In the degenerative and man-made diseases stage, there is an increase in chronic disease, but less than 50% of deaths are due to cardiovascular disease.
In the delayed degenerative diseases stage, cardiovascular disease is largely absent and cancer dominates as the primary cause of death.
The pestilence and famine stage typically has more than 50% of deaths as the result of cardiovascular disease.

answer:
The correct answer is B.

The pestilence and famine stage is the first stage of the epidemiological transition, where major causes of death include malnutrition and infectious diseases.

lectureMeta: The student-written, instructor-approved bank built by the Class of 2024 Academic Directors (December 2020) and re-filed per week by the Meds 2025 volunteers.
stem: Which of the following statements applying Emanuel’s models of the physician-patient relationship (1992) is true?

options.html: A patient presents to a family practice who trusts that the physician knows best and will follow the physician’s instructions. This patient is seeking an informative model.

A patient presents to a family practice with conflicting values about treatment options. The patient wants the physician to provide advice and counselling to arrive to the best treatment option. This patient is seeking a paternalistic model.
A patient wants to hear all the options for treating high blood pressure before making his own decision according to his own fixed values. This patient is seeking an interpretive model.

A patient comes into the clinic seeking sleeping pills. The physician attempts to convince the patient that they should first attempt a behavioural modification approach, including introducing appropriate sleep hygiene. This is an example of the deliberative model.
When a patient and physician are close friends, it’s an example of the fraternalistic model.

answer:
The correct answer is D.

In the deliberative model, the physician acts as a teacher, articulating and persuading the patient of appropriate values and treatments.

lectureMeta: The student-written, instructor-approved bank built by the Class of 2024 Academic Directors (December 2020) and re-filed per week by the Meds 2025 volunteers.
stem: Jerry has forgotten about a sum of $1000 in cash left under his mattress. His neighbour, Keith, breaks in and finds the $1000, and takes it home to feed his starving family. Because Jerry has forgotten about this, the money was never missed. Which of the following statements about Keith’s action is correct?

options.html: According to social intuitionism, it is important to understand the reasons for Keith’s actions and other contextual information before reaching a conclusion about the rightness/wrongness of the act.
If Keith was practicing casuistry, the decision to take the money would have been the result of an outside-the-box solution to his current financial problems.
To decide if there is any wrongdoing, a proponent of ethical deliberation immediately> arrives at a conclusion regarding this situation, and then finds reasons to justify it.
A deontologist would not find Keith’s actions to be wrong because the decision to take the money from Jerry treated him as an end in-and-of-himself.
According to utilitarianism, there is no wrongdoing in this situation as happiness and utility is maximized.

answer:
The correct answer is E.

In utilitarianism, actions strive to improve utility and happiness. Since Jerry has forgotten about the cash under his mattress, he will not suffer any pain if it is stolen, and this cash can help Keith and Keith’s family.

lectureMeta: The student-written, instructor-approved bank built by the Class of 2024 Academic Directors (December 2020) and re-filed per week by the Meds 2025 volunteers.
stem: Which was not a significant contribution toward the history of medicine in the Medieval period?

options.html: The printing press allowed for the dissemination of a lot of medical knowledge.
The importance of a working knowledge of anatomy was first introduced
Diagnostic tests involved examining bodily fluids, such as urine.

answer:
The correct answer is C.

The importance of anatomy in medicine was a key advancement made by Galen of Pergamum, a Greek Physician, about 150 years BCE.

lectureMeta: The student-written, instructor-approved bank built by the Class of 2024 Academic Directors (December 2020) and re-filed per week by the Meds 2025 volunteers.
stem: Which option correctly describes a type of cellular junction?

options.html: Tight junctions allow small molecule transport between the cytoplasm of adjoining cells.
Desmosomes and Adherens junctions have the same function, linking cells to interstitial fluid.
A gap junction is a reference to the extracellular fluid that forms gaps between cells when viewed by microscope.
Hemidesmosomes attach epidermis cells to a basal membrane.
Gap junctions utilize a single connexin protein to make gaps of uniform sizes.

answer:
The correct answer is D.

Hemidesmosome form connections with the basal membrane.

lectureMeta: The student-written, instructor-approved bank built by the Class of 2024 Academic Directors (December 2020) and re-filed per week by the Meds 2025 volunteers.
stem: What type of cartilage is found in the epiglottis and the larynx?
answer:
The correct answer is A.

Elastic cartilage forms epiglottis, larynx and is made of Type 2 collagen and elastin.

lectureMeta: The student-written, instructor-approved bank built by the Class of 2024 Academic Directors (December 2020) and re-filed per week by the Meds 2025 volunteers.
stem: Which option incorrectly identifies the unique features of smooth, skeletal, and cardiac muscle cells?

options.html: Cardiac muscle and smooth muscle are uni-nucleated.
Skeletal muscles are striated; smooth muscle and cardiac muscle are non- striated.
T-tubules are found only in skeletal and cardiac muscle cells.
Only cardiac muscle cells possess intercalated discs.

answer:
The correct answer is C.

Cardiac muscle is striated, like skeletal muscles.

From 05 - Muscle Tissue. The question asks for the incorrect statement. The lecture's table has skeletal and cardiac muscle as striated; only smooth muscle is not, so C is wrong.

  • A correct: cardiac and smooth muscle each have a single central nucleus (skeletal is a multinucleated syncytium with peripheral nuclei).
  • B correct: skeletal is voluntary; cardiac and smooth are involuntary.
  • D correct: T-tubules are in skeletal (triads) and cardiac (wider, at the Z line, diads); smooth muscle uses caveolae instead.
  • E correct: intercalated discs (gap junctions, adherens junctions, desmosomes) are unique to cardiac muscle.

lectureMeta: The student-written, instructor-approved bank built by the Class of 2024 Academic Directors (December 2020) and re-filed per week by the Meds 2025 volunteers.
stem: Which component of a sarcomere does not shorten upon contraction?
answer:
The correct answer is A.

The A band does not shorten during contraction.

From 05 - Muscle Tissue. The A band is the length of the thick (myosin) filaments, which stay stationary; in the sliding filament model the thin filaments slide over them, so filament lengths do not change and the A band stays constant.

  • H zone shortens: it is the thick-filament-only centre, which narrows as thin filaments slide in.
  • I band shortens: it is the thin-filament-only region, which narrows as the Z lines are pulled toward the M line.
  • U band is not a sarcomere structure (the bands are A, I, H, with Z and M lines).

stem: Which of the following is a similarity between skeletal muscle and cardiac muscle?

options.html: Both have a nucleus that is centrally located
Both use T-tubules to propagate action potentials
Both use gap junctions to transmit action potentials

answer:
The correct answer is C.

Both use T-tubules to propagate action potentials. Smooth muscle has caveolae.

lectureMeta: The student-written, instructor-approved bank built by the Class of 2024 Academic Directors (December 2020) and re-filed per week by the Meds 2025 volunteers.
stem: In Multiple Sclerosis, the immune system attacks oligodendrocytes. Which of the following are primarily affected?

options.html: Unmyelinated axons in the peripheral nervous system
Unmyelinated axons in the central nervous system
Myelinated axons in the peripheral nervous system
Myelinated axons in the central nervous system

answer:
The correct answer is D.

Oligodendrocytes myelinate cells in the CNS.

From 07 - Nerves. Oligodendrocytes myelinate axons in the central nervous system, one cell covering many axons (40-50 internodal segments); the lecture names CNS demyelination as multiple sclerosis, and because oligodendrocytes do not proliferate there is no repair.

  • C fails: myelinated PNS axons are wrapped by Schwann cells, one cell per segment of one axon - these are spared in MS.
  • A and B fail: unmyelinated axons have no myelin for an attack on myelinating cells to remove.

stem: A chemist drinks some deionized, distilled water (hypotonic to bodily fluids). Which Darrow-Yannet diagram below represents the equilibrium response after drinking the water but before the kidneys have responded?
answer:
The correct answer is B.

Hypotonic water ingestion would increase the total volume of water in the body, and decrease the osmolarity.

lectureMeta: The student-written, instructor-approved bank built by the Class of 2024 Academic Directors (December 2020) and re-filed per week by the Meds 2025 volunteers.
stem: On Superbowl Sunday, Dr. Crowley hosts all the 2024’s over for a party to teach about homeostasis. She supplies endless chips and nachos but her plumbing is broken so she cannot offer water. Which Darrow-Yannet diagram below represents the equilibrium response after eating the chips but before the kidneys have responded?
answer:
The correct answer is D.

Increased salt intake would increase osmolarity in extracellular fluid with no increase in extracellular volume. Equilibrium involves water leaving the intracellular fluid and entering the extracellular fluid. This results in increased ECF volume, decreased ICF volume, and increased osmolarity in both..

stem: Which option correctly matches the type of membrane transport with a correct example?

options.html: Osmosis is the movement of water from a cell into a hyposmotic solution.
Active transport is what brings calcium back into the sarcoplasmic reticulum after muscle contraction
Endocytosis results in the release of acetylcholine from axon terminals across the synaptic cleft.
Simple diffusion is the transport of small, charged atoms down their concentration gradient.
Facilitated diffusion moves one solute up a concentration gradient by moving another down a concentration gradient.

answer:
The correct answer is B.

Moving calcium back into the SR is an active transport process.

lectureMeta: The student-written, instructor-approved bank built by the Class of 2024 Academic Directors (December 2020) and re-filed per week by the Meds 2025 volunteers.
stem: Which statement concerning muscle contraction is true?

options.html: Calcium-bound troponin prevents actin and myosin from associating.
Calcium-bound tropomyosin allows actin and myosin to associate.
Calcium-bound troponin allows actin and tropomyosin to dissociate.
Calcium-bound actin-myosin complex initiates the power stroke.
Calcium-bound myosin allows actin, troponin, and tropomyosin to associate.

answer:
The correct answer is C.

Tropomyosin binds actin in the absence of calcium.

From 05 - Muscle Tissue. The sequence in the note: Ca2+ released from the sarcoplasmic reticulum binds troponin C, causing a conformational change that frees tropomyosin from the myosin-binding sites on actin. Myosin then binds actin and makes its power stroke. So calcium-bound troponin lets tropomyosin come away from actin (C).

  • A reverses the effect: calcium-bound troponin permits actin-myosin binding.
  • B names the wrong calcium-binding protein: calcium binds troponin, not tropomyosin.
  • D: calcium does not bind the actin-myosin complex; the power stroke is the myosin head's conformational change.
  • E: calcium does not act through myosin here, and the effect is to move tropomyosin away from actin, not bind it on.

lectureMeta: The student-written, instructor-approved bank built by the Class of 2024 Academic Directors (December 2020) and re-filed per week by the Meds 2025 volunteers.
stem: Which is not a major type of cell-to-cell communication?
answer:
The correct answer is E.

From 08 - Cellular Communication. The note's modes of cell signalling are autocrine (a cell signals itself), paracrine (short-distance messengers), cell-cell contact (mediators through gap junctions), synaptic (neurotransmitter release) and endocrine (hormones carried in the bloodstream).

  • A (synaptic), B (gap junctions), C (endocrine) and D (paracrine) are all on that list.
  • E (“uterine”) names an organ, not a signalling mode, so it is the exception. The uterus's own cells communicate through the modes above; visceral smooth muscle there uses gap junctions.

lectureMeta: The student-written, instructor-approved bank built by the Class of 2024 Academic Directors (December 2020) and re-filed per week by the Meds 2025 volunteers.
stem: Which phase of the action potential is characterized by the gradual opening of potassium voltage-gated channels and the inactivation of voltage gated sodium channels?
answer:
The correct answer is B.

During repolarization, potassium channels slowly open.

From 08 - Cellular Communication. In the lecture's sequence, after the peak at about +45 mV the V.G. K+ channels, which are slower than the Na+ channels, keep opening while the V.G. Na+ channels become inactivated; K+ rushes out and the membrane repolarizes from +45 back toward -70 mV.

  • Depolarization is driven by rapid Na+ channel opening and Na+ influx.
  • Hyperpolarization is the undershoot while K+ channels close slowly and K+ keeps leaving.
  • Resting membrane potential is set by K+ leak channels and the Na+/K+ pump, with V.G. channels in their resting configuration.

stem: Which of the following best depicts the phenomenon of anticipation in genetics?

options.html: A father who was diagnosed with Huntington’s disease at 40 years has a son who was diagnosed with Huntington’s at 30 years old
A father who was diagnosed with Huntington’s disease at 40 years of age has a son who was diagnosed with Huntington’s at 40 years old as well
A son who inherits the gene responsible for Huntington’s disease may or may not develop the disease
A son who inherits the gene responsible for Huntington’s disease from their father will develop this disease

answer:
The correct answer is A.

Anticipation is the phenomenon where the age of disease onset decreases with each generation.

lectureMeta: The student-written, instructor-approved bank built by the Class of 2024 Academic Directors (December 2020) and re-filed per week by the Meds 2025 volunteers.
stem:
Which scenarios below depict the phenomenon of the dominant negative effect in genetics?

  1. The mutated alpha chain prevents the orderly coiling of collagen
  2. A mutated CFTR gene leads to decreased reuptake of the chloride ions from sweat
  3. The disease progression of prions
answer:
The correct answer is B.

From 02 - Genetics (Week 3), with prions from 16 - How Viruses Work. A dominant negative effect is a mutant protein that disrupts the normal protein from the other allele, usually by interacting with it - “better to have no neighbour than a bad one”.

  • i fits: the lecture's own example is severe osteogenesis imperfecta, where the mutated alpha chain is incorporated and ruins orderly collagen coiling.
  • iii fits by the same logic: a prion is a misfolded protein that transmits its misfolded shape onto normal copies of the same protein.
  • ii fails: the CFTR defect in cystic fibrosis is autosomal recessive loss of function - carriers are fine because the normal copy is a backup, so nothing is poisoning it.

answer:
